blocks.text: Swahili pronunciation rests on five pure vowel sounds that never change, wherever they appear.

lines: Almost every Swahili word is stressed on the second-to-last syllable: ka-RI-bu, a-SAN-te, ha-BA-ri. Get this rhythm and you instantly sound natural.

lines: Used to greet anyone older or respected. The elder replies 'Marahaba'. Using it shows respect and people warm to you immediately.

title: Pronouns & 'To Be'
subtitle: Subject prefixes: the heart of verbs

blocks.text: Every verb carries a small prefix telling who does the action. Memorize these today.
In the present, 'is/am/are' is simply 'ni' (affirmative) or 'si' (negative) — the same for everyone.

lines: Mimi ni mwalimu — I am a teacher
Yeye si mgonjwa — He/She is not sick
Sisi ni marafiki — We are friends

quiz.prompt: Translate to Swahili: We are friends
Fill the blank: Yeye ___ mwalimu (He is a teacher)

blocks.calloutTitle: Build a verb: SUBJECT + na + STEM
blocks.intro: Swahili verbs snap together like blocks. Pick who’s doing it, keep -na- in the middle for “now”, then add the action. The stem never changes — only the front piece does. Tap the options below and watch the word build itself.

lines: Ninasoma kitabu — I'm reading a book
Anakunywa maji — He/She drinks water
Wanaenda shule — They go to school

quiz.prompt: Translate to Swahili: We are eating

blocks.intro: To say you DON’T do something, swap the subject prefix for its negative twin and change the verb’s final -a to -i. There’s no -na- in the negative present. Tap to build it:

blocks.text: A yes/no question looks just like a statement — raise your intonation, or add 'Je' at the start.

lines: Unapenda chai? — Do you like tea?
Ndiyo, ninapenda chai — Yes, I do
Hapana, sipendi chai — No, I don't

blocks.text: Nouns are sorted into classes that control prefixes on adjectives and verbs. Wonderfully regular once learned.
Verb agreement: a- (singular) / wa- (plural). Mtoto anacheza / Watoto wanacheza.
Agreement: u- (singular) / i- (plural). Mti unaanguka / Miti inaanguka.

blocks.intro: Tap a noun to see its class, its plural, and how it changes the verb.

quiz.prompt: The M-/WA- class is mainly for:
Translate to Swahili: trees (plural of mti)

blocks.text: A huge class — singular and plural usually look the SAME.

blocks.intro: Tap a noun to see its class, its plural, and how it changes the verb.

blocks.text: You now know the four core classes. Most nouns show their class in the prefix — and the plural is the biggest giveaway: make the noun plural and the new prefix names the class.

tableRows: a tree, plant or body part
an animal or a borrowed word

lines: Both people (M/WA) and plants/objects (M/MI) start with m-. Tell them apart by meaning: a PERSON is M/WA (plural wa-); a TREE or THING is M/MI (plural mi-).
mtoto → watoto (people) · mti → miti (things)
Unsure of a class? Pluralise it. wa- = M/WA, mi- = M/MI, vi-/vy- = KI/VI, ma- = JI/MA. No change at all? It's almost always N (animals & loanwords).
'Good' changes shape by class: mtu mzuri, kitabu kizuri, nyumba nzuri. Tomorrow you'll learn how.

quiz.prompt: In the N- class, the plural usually:
Translate to Swahili: chairs (plural of kiti)

blocks.text: An adjective comes AFTER the noun and wears a prefix that matches the noun's class. The easy rule: look at the noun's own prefix and echo it on the adjective — ki-tabu → ki-zuri, vi-tabu → vi-zuri, mi-ti → mi-refu, wa-tu → wa-zuri.
For most classes the adjective prefix is simply the noun's class prefix, copied across — and singular vs plural each take their own.

blocks.calloutTitle: Build a description: NOUN + prefix + adjective
blocks.intro: Pick a thing and a describing word. Watch the gold prefix copy the noun's class. Tap the speaker to hear it.

lines: People and animals take M/WA agreement no matter their class. rafiki (friend) is N-class, but: rafiki mzuri (good friend), marafiki wazuri.
mbwa mkubwa — a big dog · paka mdogo — a small cat.
* With N-class nouns the prefix blends into the sound: nyumba kubwa (big), nyumba ndefu (refu → ndefu), nyumba mbaya (baya → mbaya).
Borrowed adjectives never change at all: chai safi (clean tea), nyumba safi, kitu rahisi (a cheap thing). Also ghali, tayari, bora.
Mtoto mdogo — a small child
Vitabu vikubwa — big books
Nyumba nzuri — a beautiful house
Mti huu ni mrefu — this tree is tall

quiz.prompt: Translate to Swahili: a beautiful house

lines: Use 'na' (and) to join: 25 = ishirini na tano. 142 = mia moja arobaini na mbili.
Swahili time starts at sunrise (~6am). So 7am = saa moja (hour one of daylight); 1pm = saa saba. Convert by adding/subtracting 6.

blocks.text: A Swahili possessive has TWO parts: a stem that says whose it is (-angu = my, -ako = your…), and a short "link" in front of it that must agree with the noun's class. The stem never changes — only the link does. So "my" is wangu, yangu, changu, or langu depending on the noun.

blocks.calloutTitle: Build a possessive: NOUN + link + stem
blocks.intro: Pick a thing and an owner. Watch the gold LINK change with the noun's class while the stem (whose) stays the same. Tap 🔊 to hear it.

lines: The link agrees with the NOUN, not with the owner. "My book" and "their book" both use ch-: changu, chao.
Get the noun's class right and the link follows automatically.
Hili ni gari langu — This is my car
Rafiki yako anakuja — Your friend is coming
Watoto wao ni wadogo — Their children are small
Vitabu vyetu viko wapi? — Where are our books?

quiz.hint: vitabu is KI/VI plural → link vy-

quiz.prompt: 'kitabu' makes 'changu', so it belongs to class:

blocks.text: Swahili questions are easy: keep your normal sentence and drop in a question word. The big difference from English — the question word usually goes where the ANSWER would, which is often at the END, not the front.

lines: English moves the question word to the front ("Where do you live?"). Swahili leaves it in place: Unakaa wapi? — literally "You-live where?".
Mostly only nani (who) and kwa nini (why) start the sentence.

blocks.intro: Tap a question word to see and hear it inside a real sentence — and notice where it sits.

lines: ngapi (how many) takes a class prefix like an adjective: watu wangapi? (how many people), vitabu vingapi? (how many books).
gani (which) never changes and simply follows its noun: chai gani? (which tea?).
Jina lako ni nani? — What is your name? (lit. your name is who?)
Unatoka wapi? — Where are you from?
Ni saa ngapi? — What time is it? (how many hours?)
Kwa nini unajifunza Kiswahili? — Why are you learning Swahili?

quiz.prompt: In Swahili, where does the question word usually go?
options: Where the answer would go (often the end)
quiz.answer: Where the answer would go (often the end)

blocks.text: Consolidate Week 2 by describing people and things.

lines: 'To have' = 'to be with': nina (I have), una (you have), ana (he/she has), tuna, mna, wana. Nina watoto wawili — I have two children.

blocks.text: Huyu ni rafiki yangu. Jina lake ni Asha. Yeye ni mwalimu. Ana watoto wawili. Watoto wake ni wadogo lakini wazuri sana.
(This is my friend. Her name is Asha. She is a teacher. She has two children. Her children are small but very lovely.)

blocks.intro: Drag the words into the right order, then tap Check. Get it right to hear it spoken — pole pole!

quiz.prompt: Fill: ___ rafiki yangu (he/she has a friend)

blocks.calloutTitle: Build the past: SUBJECT + li + STEM
blocks.intro: Past tense is the easiest swap of all — keep everything from the present, but change the middle piece from -na- to -li-. The stem still never changes. Tap to build it:

lines: Jana nilienda sokoni — Yesterday I went to the market
Sikuona rafiki yangu — I didn't see my friend

quiz.prompt: Translate to English: jana nilienda sokoni
quiz.answer: yesterday I went to the market

blocks.calloutTitle: Build the future: SUBJECT + ta + STEM
blocks.intro: Planning ahead? Swap the tense marker to -ta-. Same subject prefixes, same unchanging stem. Tap to build it:

lines: The verb 'go' is irregular: -kwenda in most tenses (nitakwenda) but -enda in present (ninaenda).
Kesho nitakwenda sokoni — Tomorrow I'll go to market
Sitakunywa kahawa usiku — I won't drink coffee at night

quiz.prompt: Translate to Swahili: I will eat
Translate to Swahili: They will travel tomorrow

blocks.text: Shows a completed action with present relevance.

blocks.calloutTitle: Build the perfect: SUBJECT + me + STEM
blocks.intro: “Have done” uses -me-. Same build pattern, new marker — it signals a finished action that still matters now. Tap to build it:

blocks.text: Negative perfect uses -ja- ('not yet'): Sijala — I haven't eaten yet.
For general habits, use hu- with NO subject prefix: Hunywa chai kila asubuhi — (generally) drink tea every morning.

quiz.prompt: Translate to Swahili: I have arrived

blocks.text: Example: Stesheni iko wapi? — Endelea moja kwa moja, kisha geukia kushoto.

quiz.prompt: Translate to English: hoteli iko wapi

blocks.text: Add -ni to mean 'at/in/on/to' that place.

lines: Kuna chakula mezani — There is food on the table
Hakuna maji — There is no water
Niko nyumbani — I am at home
Uko wapi? — Where are you?

quiz.prompt: Translate to Swahili: Where are you? (uko ...)

blocks.text: You now have all four core tenses. Today you weave them into a narrative.

Jana niliamka asubuhi. Kwanza nilikunywa chai, kisha nilienda sokoni. Nilinunua matunda. Baadaye nilirudi nyumbani na nilipika chakula. Jioni nilikuwa nimechoka, kwa hiyo nililala mapema. Kesho nitafanya kazi.
(Yesterday I woke up. First I drank tea, then went to market. I bought fruit. Later I returned home and cooked. In the evening I was tired, so I slept early. Tomorrow I'll work.)

quiz.prompt: Translate to Swahili: I woke up (ni + li + amka)

blocks.intro: For wishes, suggestions and “should”, drop the tense marker entirely and change the verb’s final -a to -e. Tap to build it:

blocks.text: After taka (want) and lazima (must), the next verb is subjunctive: Nataka uende — I want you to go. Lazima tusome — We must study.

quiz.prompt: In the subjunctive, the final -a changes to:

title: Object Infixes
subtitle: Pack the object into the verb

blocks.calloutTitle: Slot the object in: SUBJECT + na + OBJECT + STEM
blocks.intro: Swahili tucks the object pronoun INSIDE the verb, right before the stem. Pick a subject, an object, and a verb to watch it snap together:

lines: Nilimwona jana — I saw him/her yesterday
Watakusaidia — They will help you

blocks.text: There's also a tighter infixed form: Mtu anayesoma... / Kitabu nilichonunua... Start with amba- forms; they always work.
